text: California's one-call law is Government Code 4216 to 4216.24. There are two regional notification centers: Underground Service Alert of Southern California (DigAlert, digalert.org) and USA North 811 (usanorth811.org) for the rest of the state; dialing 811 or going online reaches the right one. Process: (1) delineate (white-line) the dig area before you call (4216.2(a)); (2) file the ticket at least 2 working days before digging, not counting the day you call, and not more than 14 calendar days before (4216.2(b)) (a Monday call means Thursday is the first dig day); (3) operators mark their lines or report no conflict by the legal start date and post an electronic positive response you can check on the ticket (4216.3); (4) inside the tolerance zone (24 inches each side of the mark) find the line with hand tools, or vacuum excavation if the operator agreed, before any power equipment (4216.4); (5) the ticket is good for 28 days; renew by the end of the 28th day or stop digging (4216.2(e), (i)). Private lines past the operator's service point are not marked. This is a plain-language summary; the law and the center's excavator manual govern.
title: California 811: DigAlert and USA North, how a locate request works (Gov Code 4216)
topic: Utility locates in California: Gov Code 4216, DigAlert and USA North 811
source: California Government Code 4216, 4216.2, 4216.3, 4216.4 (as amended through Jan. 1, 2025); DigAlert and USA North 811 excavator guidance

text: Arizona's dig law is A.R.S. 40-360.21 to 40-360.32, enforced by the Arizona Corporation Commission. One center: Arizona 811. Mark the dig area with white lining before you call (40-360.22(C)); a person digging on a single-family home lot is excused. Operators must mark "as promptly as practicable, but not later than two working days"; Arizona 811 calls these two full working days, so a Monday call means Thursday is the first dig day if every operator has answered. Working days skip Saturday, Sunday, legal holidays and the Friday after Thanksgiving. You may not start "before the location and marking are complete or the excavator is notified that marking is unnecessary." Marks are good for 15 working days from the date of marking. If work goes on, give notice at least 2 working days before they run out. Within 24 inches of a marked line, expose it carefully with hand tools and support it. Hit a line: tell the operator right away; gas or hazardous material, also call 911. Leave the hole open until the operator arrives. Fine: up to $5,000 per violation.

text: Arkansas's dig law is the Arkansas Underground Facilities Damage Prevention Act, Ark. Code 14-271-101 and after. One center: Arkansas 811. Notice (14-271-112): "at least two (2), but not more than ten (10), full working days before commencing" the dig (a Monday call means Thursday is the first dig day). The notice is "effective for a period of twenty (20) working days from the date that the notice was given." Work not finished or marks gone: "reinitiate the notice procedure," which means calling it in again with the normal wait. The tolerance zone, white lining rule, damage steps and fine amounts were not read in this pass and are not confirmed here. Until they are: hand dig or vacuum to find any marked line before a machine works near it, and if you hit a line call the owner, and 911 if gas or liquid is escaping.

text: Colorado's dig law is C.R.S. 9-1.5-101 to 9-1.5-108, with the Underground Damage Prevention Safety Commission hearing violations. One center: Colorado 811. Notice: "at least two (2) full business days prior to any excavation," not counting the call day (a Monday call means Thursday is the first dig day). Marks are good for 30 days from the ticket's due date, or until you can't see them, whichever is first. To go on, notify Colorado 811 at least 2 business days before the 30 days end; once it has run out you need a new ticket. Tolerance zone: the width of the line plus 18 inches on each side. Use non-destructive digging there (hand or vacuum). Check that every member on the ticket has posted a positive response before you dig. If one has not by the locate-by date, send an Excavator Re-Notification first. Hit a line: stop, notify 811 and the operator right away; gas release, clear the area and call 911.

text: Florida's dig law is chapter 556, the Underground Facility Damage Prevention and Safety Act. One center: Sunshine 811. Notice: "not less than 2 full business days before beginning any excavation" (a Monday call means Thursday is the first dig day) (10 full business days for underwater work). A ticket is valid for 30 calendar days. Not finished: give another notice for the part still to dig. Tolerance zone: 24 inches from the outer edge of either side of the marked line. Inside it, "use increased caution": hand dig, pothole, soft dig or vacuum. You must check the positive responses before you dig. Pre-mark in white when the site can't otherwise be identified. Hit a line: "immediately notify the member operator"; if gas or a hazardous substance escapes, call 911. Citations are $500 plus court costs, $2,500 for hazardous material pipelines.
title: Florida 811 rules in short: wait before you dig, how long a ticket is good, hand-dig zone (Sunshine 811)

text: Illinois's dig law is the Underground Utility Facilities Damage Prevention Act, 220 ILCS 50, rewritten effective January 1, 2025 and enforced by the Illinois Commerce Commission. JULIE is the one-call center everywhere outside the City of Chicago; Chicago runs its own system (811 Chicago). Notice: "not less than 2 days but no more than 10 days in advance." A "day" skips Saturdays, Sundays, JULIE holidays and the day of the notice (a Monday call means Thursday is the first dig day). A normal notice is good for 25 days from the first request. An extension can be asked for from day 20 and adds 25 days. Pre-mark the dig area in white (black when there is snow on the ground). Since January 1, 2026: confirm every notified operator has posted a positive response before you dig. Tolerance zone: one and one-half feet (18 inches) on either side of the outside edge of the marked line. Hit a line: notify the owner and JULIE right away; gas or hazardous material escaping, call 911.

text: Kansas's dig law is the Kansas Underground Utility Damage Prevention Act, K.S.A. 66-1801 to 66-1816, enforced by the Kansas Corporation Commission. One center: Kansas 811. Notice: "at least two full working days but not more than 20 calendar days before the scheduled excavation start date." (a Monday call means Thursday is the first dig day) The notice, or any update, is "valid for 20 calendar days after the excavation start date" (changed from 15 days on January 1, 2024). Ticket only what you can reasonably finish in that time. To go on, update the notice. Do not make repeated remark requests unless the cause was out of your control; the Commission has warned of fines for needless updates. Whiteline the dig area when the operator asks for it. Pre-engineered and permitted projects still need the notice before digging starts. The tolerance zone (24 inches in K.S.A. 66-1802) and fine amounts were not re-read today and are not confirmed here.

text: Kentucky's dig law is the Underground Facility Damage Prevention Act, KRS 367.4901 to 367.4917. One center: Kentucky 811. Notice: "not less than two (2) full working days nor more than ten (10) full working days prior to commencing work" (a Monday call means Thursday is the first dig day). "Locate requests are valid for twenty-one (21) calendar days from the day of the initial request." Ask for remarking two working days before each 21-day period ends, or sooner if the marks are gone or the plan changes. Mark the edges of the dig yourself when an operator asks or the area can't be described. Operator did not respond in time: "the excavator shall submit a second notice." If there is still nothing one working day later, an excavator who followed the law is not liable for damage to lines that would have been located (not true for certain gas and hazardous liquid pipelines). Inside the tolerance zone, "hand-dig or use nonintrusive means." Machines are allowed for pavement, rock, and material more than 12 inches in any direction from the located line, with a watcher. Hit a line: stop and notify the operators; flammable, toxic or corrosive escape, call 911.

text: Missouri's dig law is the Underground Facility Safety and Damage Prevention Act, RSMo 319.010 to 319.050 (amended August 28, 2025). One center: Missouri 811. Notice: "at least two working days, but not more than ten working days, before the expected date" of starting. A notice is good until 11:59 p.m. 21 consecutive calendar days from the start date of work on the ticket (RSMo 319.025, amended by 2025 SB 133); work while the marks can be seen until then. If you can't start within ten working days, make a relocate request before digging. Marks unusable: ask the center for a remark. White lining (paint, stakes, whiskers) may be used when the site can't be clearly described. Find a line unmarked or marked wrong: notify the center; the owner must contact you or mark it correctly within two hours. Hand or soft digging "shall be used as a best practice when possible"; no hand-dig distance is given in this section. Hit a line: notify the center. Gas or hazardous liquid pipeline release: "immediately contact 911." Do not hide or repair damage without the owner's OK.
title: Missouri 811 rules in short: wait before you dig, how long a ticket is good, hand-dig zone (Missouri 811)

text: Nevada's dig law is NRS 455.080 to 455.180 with rules in NAC 455. One center: USA North 811. Call at least 2 working days (7 AM to 5 PM, not weekends or holidays, call day not counted) and not more than 28 calendar days before digging (a Monday call means Thursday is the first dig day). Mark the dig area in white first. Wait for every operator: the handbook says excavators "are required by law to wait until all operators" have given a positive response, even if the start time on the ticket has passed. A ticket is good for 28 calendar days from the date and time of the notification. It can be extended twice, 28 days each; after that the regulation requires a new notification (NAC 455.165). That is 84 days at most on one ticket. Hand tools only within 24 inches on either side of the outside of the line. Hit a line: notify the operator right away; in an emergency also 911.
title: Nevada 811 rules in short: wait before you dig, how long a ticket is good, hand-dig zone (USA North 811)

text: New Mexico's dig law is the Excavation Damage to Pipelines and Underground Utility Lines Act (NMSA 62-14) with rule 18.60.5 NMAC, enforced by the Public Regulation Commission's pipeline safety bureau. One center: NM811. Notice: 2 working days, not counting the day you call (a Monday call means Thursday is the first dig day); operators must mark "within two full working days from the effective date of the ticket." Marks are good for 15 working days from the end of the notice period. Marks gone with no offsets: stop and ask for a relocate, only for the part still to dig, and say why. Jobs longer than 15 working days: ask for a wide area conference at least two working days ahead, write a work plan signed by all, and reaffirm the wide area ticket every 15 working days. Pre-mark in white: it shows the actual dig, not the limits of construction. Before digging, check that every operator has marked or cleared. If one has not, call for a warning locate. Within 18 inches either side of a mark, expose the line first by non-mechanical means or vacuum. Hit a line: stop, call 911 if needed, the operator and 811, secure the site, and stay until released.
title: New Mexico 811 rules in short: wait before you dig, how long a ticket is good, hand-dig zone (NM811)

text: New York's dig rules are 16 NYCRR Part 753 ("Code Rule 753") under General Business Law Article 36, enforced by the Public Service Commission. Two centers: UDig NY upstate and New York 811 for New York City and Long Island. Notice: "at least two but not more than ten working days, not including the date of the call." (a Monday call means Thursday is the first dig day) There is no ticket expiry date. If you put the start off by more than ten working days, give a new notice. Do not start until you have heard from "each and every operator" that its lines are marked or that it has none. Use the Automated Positive Response system where there is one. Tolerance zone: half the known diameter plus two feet on each side of the center line (two feet each side if the size is not known). Verify the line's exact location before power equipment goes in the zone; gas and liquid petroleum lines must be found with hand-dug test holes. Hit a line: tell the operator right away; gas, liquid or electric emergency, clear the area and call 911.

text: Ohio's dig law is O.R.C. 3781.25 to 3781.38 (amended June 9, 2026); complaints go to the Underground Technical Committee at the PUCO. One center: OHIO811. Oil and gas producers answer through a separate group reached by the same call. Notice: "at least two working days, not including the day of the notification," and "not more than sixteen calendar days before commencing excavation." (a Monday call means Thursday is the first dig day) The law and the June 2026 manual give no ticket expiry date. Keep the ticket for the whole job and ask for a remark when marks fade. Premark the dig in white paint unless an exception applies. Check Positive Response before you go to the job; code 999 means an owner has not answered by the legal start. Tolerance zone: the width of the line plus 18 inches on each side. Dig there carefully, with a second person watching the bucket. Hit a line: get everyone safe, stop, notify the utility and OHIO811; anything flammable, toxic or corrosive escaping, call 911.
title: Ohio 811 rules in short: wait before you dig, how long a ticket is good, hand-dig zone (OHIO811)

text: Oregon's dig rules are ORS 757.542 to 757.562 and OAR chapter 952, written by the Oregon Utility Notification Center (Oregon 811). Pre-mark the dig area in white, then call at least 2 full business days and not more than 10 business days before digging (a Monday call means Thursday is the first dig day). Do not start until you have "received a response from each operator of underground facilities in the area." Ticket life: 30 calendar days. The Center's 2026 Addendum says the rule was changed "from 45 days to 30 days," effective January 8, 2026, and Oregon 811's own homeowner page says marks should no longer be used after 30 days. Older copies of the rule still say 45. Past ticket life, call in a new locate request. Tolerance zone: 24 inches around the outside of the line on all sides. Use hand tools or other non-invasive methods there. Hit a line: tell the operator right away; gas or hazardous liquid release, call 911. Don't bury it without the operator's OK.
title: Oregon 811 rules in short: wait before you dig, how long a ticket is good, hand-dig zone (Oregon 811)

text: Washington's dig law is RCW 19.122, enforced by the Utilities and Transportation Commission (UTC). Mark the boundary of the dig "with white lining or, when necessary, white pin flags," then call 811. Notice: "not less than two full business days and not more than 10 full business days" before the work-to-begin date (a Monday call means Thursday is the first dig day). Since January 1, 2026 you "may not commence excavation until the excavator has received positive response" from every operator with lines in the area. Marks expire 45 calendar days after you gave notice; to dig after that, give a new notice. Marks are accurate to within 24 inches of the outside of the line on both sides. Find the exact location before digging there: hand digging when practical, vacuum or air tools. Hit a line: tell the operator and 811, call 911 if it is an emergency, don't bury it, and report the damage to the UTC within 45 days.
title: Washington 811 rules in short: wait before you dig, how long a ticket is good, hand-dig zone (Washington 811)
topic: 811 dig rules by state: wait before digging, ticket life, tolerance zone
edition: RCW as amended through Laws of 2025 chapter 292

text: West Virginia's dig law is W. Va. Code Chapter 24C. One center: West Virginia 811. Notice: "Not less than forty-eight hours, excluding Saturdays, Sundays and federal or state legal holidays," and not more than ten work days before work begins. Changing the start date or time: tell the one-call system at least 24 hours ahead, not counting weekends and holidays. West Virginia 811's 2026 training, quoting the statute: a ticket is valid no more than 15 business days (no weekends or holidays) and the tolerance zone is 2 feet from the outside edge of the line (not confirmed in the statute text). Each equipment operator must be told to avoid damage, "including hand digging, when necessary," to keep a clearance "as may be reasonably necessary" from lines given the reach of the cutting edge, to protect marks and stakes, and to support lines during work and backfill. Line hit: report it immediately and give the operator reasonable time to repair. An emergency: alert the public and call 911. Damage that is not an emergency: notify the one-call system within 24 hours. Failing to notify or to report is a misdemeanor with a fine of "not more than $5,000," and you owe the repair cost.
title: West Virginia 811 rules in short: wait before you dig, how long a ticket is good, hand-dig zone (West Virginia 811)

text: Wyoming's dig law is the Wyoming Underground Facilities Notification Act, Wyo. Stat. 37-12-301 to 37-12-307. One center: One-Call of Wyoming (811). Notice: "at least two (2) full business days, but not more than fourteen (14) business days prior to any excavation." (a Monday call means Thursday is the first dig day) A job that runs longer than 14 business days needs the notice given again for each following 14 business day period. Mark the dig area before the locator comes, unless one operator can find the site from the address, there was a site meeting, or it is an emergency. Operators mark "within twenty-four (24) inches horizontally" of the outside of the line, in APWA colors, within two full business days. Reasonable care is always required, and it calls for hand or soft digging where needed to protect the line. Hit or touch a line: notify the operator and the center immediately. Gas or hazardous liquid released: call 911 first. Do not hide damage or repair it without authorization. In a dispute the excavator has to prove reasonable care. If the operator missed its deadline or marked wrong, an excavator who used reasonable care is not liable. Penalty amounts were not confirmed.
title: Wyoming 811 rules in short: wait before you dig, how long a ticket is good, hand-dig zone (One-Call of Wyoming)

text: Washington has one confined space rule for all industries, chapter 296-809 WAC, instead of the federal construction rule; OSHA's adoption table lists it as different but at least as effective. Oxygen and flammable limits match federal: flammables over 10 percent of the LFL or LEL, oxygen below 19.5 or above 23.5 percent (296-809-099); carbon monoxide is stricter in Washington, 35 ppm (WAC 296-841-20025). Its definitions add: any physical hazard (electrical shock, moving parts) makes a space permit-required; where the opening is big enough to fully enter, a permit is needed even for partial body entry; excavations and pits are among its examples. Permit (read 2026-11-19): the same 15 items as the federal general industry list, in another order (296-809-50004), with equipment to detect a rise in hazard if ventilation stops (federal construction item (e)); available at entry (50002(5)); problems noted on it (50002(7)); kept 1 year (50006(2)). Air is tested with a calibrated, direct-reading instrument (60004(3)(a)). The app's permit form covers these items.
title: Washington confined space rule (chapter 296-809 WAC): one rule for all industries
topic: State safety plan: confined space

text: 29 CFR 1904.39(a): report to OSHA within 8 hours after the death of any employee from a work-related incident, and within 24 hours after the in-patient hospitalization of one or more employees, an amputation, or the loss of an eye. How: call or go to the nearest OSHA Area Office, call 1-800-321-OSHA (1-800-321-6742), or use the online form at osha.gov. A voicemail, fax or email to a closed office does not count. A death is reportable only if it occurs within 30 days of the incident; a hospitalization, amputation or eye loss only if it occurs within 24 hours of the incident. If you learn of it later, the clock starts when you or your agent learn. In-patient hospitalization means formal admission for care or treatment; admission only for observation or tests is not reportable. Sent home from the emergency room (ER) without being admitted: no OSHA call for that (it may still go on the 300 log). A motor vehicle crash on a public road is reportable only if it happened in a construction work zone. All employers report, even those exempt from keeping the OSHA 300 log. Many state plans use shorter times or longer lists, so check the job's state.
title: Reporting a death, a worker admitted to the hospital, an amputation or eye loss to federal OSHA: 8 and 24 hours
topic: Injury reporting and OSHA recordkeeping

text: California employers report to Cal/OSHA (the Division of Occupational Safety and Health) immediately, by telephone or the online mechanism, any serious injury or illness, or death, of an employee at work (8 CCR 342(a)). "Immediately means as soon as practically possible but not longer than 8 hours after the employer knows" or with diligent inquiry would have known. Only if the employer can show exigent circumstances may the report be made within 24 hours of the incident. Serious injury or illness (8 CCR 330(h)) means a hospital admission as an inpatient for more than observation or tests, an amputation, the loss of an eye, or serious permanent disfigurement; a crash on a public road counts only in a construction zone. Taken to the emergency room (ER) and admitted: call Cal/OSHA within 8 hours; an ER visit only for observation or tests is not by itself a serious injury. The report gives the time and date, employer name and contact, the site address, the injured person's name, the nature of the injury, where the person was taken, and a description of the accident and whether the scene was changed. The federal 24 hours for a hospitalization does not apply to a job covered by Cal/OSHA.
title: California injury reporting: serious injury or worker in the hospital, immediately and no later than 8 hours
topic: State safety plan: injury reporting

text: Minnesota (MNOSHA) uses the federal confined space in construction rule, 29 CFR 1926 Subpart AA: the old state construction rule, Minn. R. 5207.0300 to 5207.0304, is marked repealed (42 SR 1015; read 2026-11-19). MNOSHA's page of differences from federal OSHA lists nothing for confined space or excavation. Trenches in this state follow the federal excavation rule, 29 CFR 1926.651 and 1926.652: protection from 5 ft, or shallower when a competent person sees signs of a possible cave-in; MNOSHA's trenching fact sheet states no state difference (read by an earlier check on 2026-11-20).

text: Nevada OSHA has incorporated most federal OSHA standards by reference, according to OSHA's page for the state's plan. Its unique standards listed there are, for construction, cranes, steel erection and asbestos, and for general industry, safety programs, explosives, sanitation and hazard communication. Excavation and confined space are not on the list, so trench protection is the federal 5 ft rule (29 CFR 1926.652) and confined space in construction is 29 CFR 1926 Subpart AA. A written safety program is required of employers with more than 10 employees (NRS 618.383, as described in Nevada OSHA's heat guidance). Injury reporting to Nevada OSHA uses the federal times: a death within 8 hours; a hospitalization, amputation or eye loss within 24 hours (Nevada OSHA's report page). Federal OSHA covers military bases, land under exclusive federal jurisdiction and tribal land.
title: Nevada: federal rules by reference, plus state safety program rules
topic: State safety plan: who enforces and what differs

text: South Carolina OSHA has identically adopted the federal standards, according to OSHA's page for the plan, with two unique construction items: excavations and general safety and health requirements. The state's list of changes to 29 CFR 1926 shows the excavation change in the definition of competent person (1926.650(b)): besides being able to identify existing and predictable hazards and having authority to correct them, the competent person "must have specific training in, and be knowledgeable about, soils analysis, the use of protective systems" and the requirements of the excavation rule. Federal OSHA says that only in its preamble. Everything else is the federal rule: protection from 5 ft (29 CFR 1926.652), ladder at 4 ft within 25 ft, spoil 2 ft back. The comparison document shows two versions of the definition side by side; reading the first as the state's is our reading of its column order, so that point is not confirmed with the agency. Injury reporting to SC OSHA uses the federal times: 8 hours for a death, 24 hours for a hospitalization, amputation or eye loss (SC OSHA's report page).
title: South Carolina trench rule: federal text, with training written into competent person
topic: State safety plan: trench and excavation
source: SC OSHA, SC 1926 standard modifications (1926.650(b)); OSHA South Carolina State Plan page

text: There is no federal 811 wait time, ticket life or tolerance zone: each state's one-call law sets its own numbers. The federal floor everywhere is 49 CFR 196 for digging near pipelines: use one-call first, wait for the marks, dig with care, report damage, call 911 for a release. Ticket life, from each state's card (use only the job state's line; day type as its card says). 14 days: Minnesota, Oklahoma, Texas (working days). 15: Arizona, District of Columbia, New Mexico, South Carolina, Tennessee, Virginia. 20: Alabama, Arkansas, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Mississippi. 21: Kentucky, Michigan, Missouri (from the start date), North Dakota, South Dakota, Utah. 25: Iowa, Illinois. 28: California, Hawaii, Nevada, North Carolina. 30: Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Oregon, Vermont, Connecticut (app table, not confirmed). 4 weeks: Idaho. 45: New Jersey (business days), Washington. 60: Maine. 12 business days: Delaware, Maryland. 15 business days: West Virginia. Each 14 business days: Wyoming. No set expiry: Alaska, New York, Rhode Island (while marks are kept up), Wisconsin, Ohio (none given, not confirmed). Not confirmed: Montana, Nebraska, Pennsylvania.
title: 811 ticket life by state: how long is a locate ticket good for in my state?
topic: 811 dig rules by state: wait before digging, ticket life, tolerance zone

text: There is no federal 811 wait time, ticket life or tolerance zone: each state's one-call law sets its own numbers. The federal floor everywhere is 49 CFR 196 for digging near pipelines: use one-call first, wait for the marks, dig with care, report damage, call 911 for a release. Tolerance zone, from each state's card (use only the job state's line; measured from the mark, the edge or plus the line's width as its card says). 18 inches: Alabama (from 2027), Colorado, District of Columbia, Georgia, Illinois, Iowa, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland (not re-read), Massachusetts, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Dakota, Vermont, Wisconsin, Texas (pipelines, plus half the diameter). 24 inches or 2 feet: Alaska, Arizona, California, Delaware, Florida, Idaho, Minnesota, Nevada, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Oregon, South Carolina, Utah, Washington, West Virginia, Wyoming; Kansas, New Jersey, Tennessee, Virginia (in the statute, not re-read). 48 inch caution zone: Michigan. Not confirmed: Arkansas, Connecticut, Hawaii, Indiana, Kentucky, Missouri, Montana.

text: Twenty-one states run their own OSHA plan for private construction crews. A plan must be at least as effective as federal OSHA's confined space in construction rule (29 CFR 1926 Subpart AA) and may be stricter, so name the plan as the source. Use only the line for the job's state. As checked by 2026-11-21. Uses the federal rule, no state change found: Alaska (8 AAC 61.1010(c)), Indiana (from Feb 4, 2016), Iowa (875 IAC 26.1), Kentucky (803 KAR 2:445), Maryland (by reference from Jan 2, 2017), Michigan (Part 35, except as amended), Minnesota, New Mexico, South Carolina (from Aug 28, 2015), Tennessee, Utah, Vermont (Vt. rule 24-050-003), Virginia, Wyoming (WY OSHA chapter 27). Vermont also keeps its own air contaminant table for general industry (CO 35 ppm over 8 hours); whether it reaches construction is not confirmed: ask VOSHA. Not on the plan's unique list, so taken as federal: Arizona, Nevada, North Carolina, Hawaii (not confirmed). Own rule, each has its own card: California (8 CCR 1950 to 1962, amended January 1, 2026, stricter CO limit), Washington (chapter 296-809, all industries; CO 35 ppm), Oregon (437-002-0146; supervisor signs, not initials).

title: Washington air limits for manholes and vaults: CO 35 ppm (stricter than federal 50 ppm), H2S 10 and 15 ppm
topic: State safety plan: confined space
text: Washington's exposure limits for airborne contaminants (WAC 296-841-20025, Table 3) apply wherever employees are or could be exposed (WAC 296-841-100), so they reach trench, manhole and vault work. Carbon monoxide: 35 ppm 8-hour average, a 200 ppm short-term limit averaged over 5 minutes, and a 1,500 ppm ceiling. The federal construction limit for carbon monoxide is 50 ppm (29 CFR 1926.55), so on a Washington job the stricter 35 ppm applies. Hydrogen sulfide: 10 ppm 8-hour average and a 15 ppm short-term limit (15 minutes); federal construction is 10 ppm. Oxygen (19.5 to 23.5 percent) and flammables (10 percent of the LEL) are the same as federal (WAC 296-809-099). A company program may set stricter alarm points. These numbers do not decide entry: the entry supervisor does, once testing, ventilation, the attendant and rescue are in place.

title: Power line contact emergency: machine touched or hit a line, stay in the cab, keep everyone back, call the power company
topic: Power lines: contact with equipment, what to do
text: If the boom, dump bed or load hits, touches or snags an overhead power line or service wire, or the machine rips into a buried electric line, treat the machine and the ground around it as live. OSHA's power line rule for equipment (29 CFR 1926.1408(g)) lists what crews must be trained on for a contact: the operator stays inside the cab unless fire, explosion or another emergency forces them out; touching the machine and the ground at the same time can electrocute; leave by the safest way (the usual method: jump clear with feet together, never touching machine and ground at once, then shuffle or hop away with feet together); the ground around the machine can be energized (step potential); the rest of the crew stays away from the machine and the load. Lines are presumed energized and uninsulated unless the utility confirms otherwise (1926.1408(g)(1)(ii)-(iii)). Call 911 and the power company to shut the line off. Do not touch a shocked person until the power is off; then CPR and an AED if they are not breathing. Report damage to a buried line to its owner and 811 as your state requires.
source: 29 CFR 1926.1408(g)(1)(i)(A)-(F), (g)(1)(ii)-(iii); the jump-and-shuffle method is common utility training, not rule text

title: Hit a gas line (nicked, ripped, blowing): what to do and who to call first
topic: 811: damage and gas line strikes
text: Any damage to a pipeline from digging, even a nick, gouge or scraped coating with no leak, must be reported promptly to the pipeline operator (49 CFR 196.107). If gas or hazardous liquid is escaping, the excavator must promptly call 911 (49 CFR 196.109). Steps crews are taught at a gas strike: get everyone out and well away, upwind; leave the machine where it is and do not restart engines near the leak; no smoking, flames or anything that sparks; do not try to crimp, plug or bury the line; keep the public and traffic back; call 911 from a safe distance, then the gas company (the operator: number on the locate ticket, or call 811); let the gas company shut it in; nobody goes back into the trench until the fire department or gas company says it is clear. Then report the damage to 811 or the operator as your state's one-call law requires, with the ticket number and photos taken from a safe distance.
source: 49 CFR 196.107 (damage report to the operator), 49 CFR 196.109 (call 911 on a release); crew steps: common gas operator damage guidance
